text: Random numbers are one of the most useful tools in data science. You use them to split data into training and test sets, to create fake data for practice, to shuffle, to sample, and to simulate — answering 'what would happen if' by running an experiment thousands of times on the computer instead of working out a formula by hand. This lesson closes out the NumPy chapter.

Modern NumPy uses a generator object. Create one with np dot random dot default underscore r-n-g, passing a seed — 42 here — and call methods on it. rng dot random of 3 gives three floats between 0 and 1. The seed picks the starting point of what's actually a formula producing pseudo-random numbers, so creating a new generator with that same seed gives you the identical sequence back. Setting a seed makes your analysis reproducible, so a teammate, or you next month, gets the same numbers.

rng dot integers from 1 to 7 gives dice rolls from 1 to 6 — the upper bound is excluded, just like range. rng dot normal with a loc of 100 and a scale of 15 draws from the bell curve you'll study in the statistics chapter, where loc and scale are its mean and standard deviation. rng dot uniform between 10 and 20 spreads evenly across that range, and rng dot exponential gives skewed data, useful for things like order values.

Choice picks from an array. By default it samples with replacement, so the same item can appear more than once — pass replace equals False to sample without repeats, and p to weight the choices, like a coin that lands heads 70 percent of the time. rng dot permutation of 5 gives you a shuffled copy of 0 through 4. Random train-test splits are built on exactly this idea: shuffle the row numbers, then cut.

What's the chance two dice add up to 7? You could count it out — 6 of 36 outcomes, 0.1667 — or you can simulate it. Roll two dice 100,000 times as a 100000-by-2 array, sum across each row with axis equals 1 from last lesson, and take the mean of the boolean array rolls equals equals 7. Because True counts as 1, that mean is the fraction of rolls that landed on 7 — 0.16775, very close to the exact answer. More trials bring the estimate even closer to the truth.

The same trick works for business questions where the math gets awkward. If each customer has an assumed 15 percent chance of churning, rng dot random of 1000 compared less-than 0.15 simulates a group of 1,000 customers, and summing that boolean array counts how many left. With seed 1 that came to 143 customers — a different seed gives a slightly different count, which shows the natural variation you should expect from any simulation.

Most simulations follow the same four steps. First, define the random process — what's actually random here. Second, repeat it many times, using arrays rather than a slow Python loop. Third, summarize the results, often as the mean of a boolean array. And fourth, check the simulation against a case where you already know the exact answer, the way we checked the dice simulation against 6 over 36.

Draw 2,000 samples of 50 orders each from a skewed population, and average each sample. The sample means cluster tightly around the true average, and their spread, about 7.07, closely matches theory — the population standard deviation divided by the square root of 50, about 7.02. That match is the idea behind the central limit theorem, which later lessons develop in full.

That same idea enables the bootstrap: with only one small sample, resample it with replacement many times and see how much the mean moves. Take eight illustrative order values, resample them 5,000 times with replacement, and average each resample. The mean of the original eight is 14.625, and the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile range of all those resampled means — roughly 12 to 17.375 — gives a rough 95 percent interval for the true mean. Treat it as an illustration of the method, not a rigorous result from only eight values.

To recap: rng equals np dot random dot default underscore r-n-g of a seed gives reproducible random numbers. Use random, integers, normal, and uniform to draw values, and choice, shuffle, and permutation to sample and reorder. Simulate by running an experiment many times in one array and taking the mean of a boolean. Bootstrap by resampling your data with replacement.
